source: I'll arrange a meeting soon. We ought to notify them as soon as we can.
Good. Let's not wait a moment longer than we have to.
(Even if this world can only last a little longer...)
(For now I can pretend, at least. Can't I?)
(Surely I haven't lost every ability to feel.)
I don't think I can, Hamlet.
So when you said you... wanted to begin things again, did you... mean it?
I did then. But that's all it was.
I gave you the push you needed to become king. And you will. You'll be magnificent.
You'll be the best King Denmark has ever had. I believe that with all my soul.
But I don't know if I can give you the rest of my life. I'm not ready to do that much.
Right, then.
I hope you won't mind if I pick up my bruised pride and leave you be.
I believe you. And so am I. But I need to be alone now.
Farewell, Ophelia.
(This world can only last a little longer...)
(The fewer feelings I have, the more effective I'll be.)
(Solving my way out of the loop is all that matters now.)
Laertes? What is it?
Come with me. Quickly.
Laertes? What is all of this?
Thank you all for gathering here tonight.
...All of you are faithful to your respective lords.
But I have a new request of you.
Of course, I wouldn't call you unless I had a desperate message for the men you serve.
...Soon, all of them will be called to elect the next King of Denmark.
My request is simple. I beseech them not to elect Hamlet, no matter what transpires.
Although Hamlet may be his father's son, I urge you to consider the cost this family has had upon our nation.
Bloodiness begets bloodiness. Death begets death.
Shall we wager our country upon the fruit newly borne off that poisoned tree?
Or shall we rise up and declare a new, prosperous direction of our own making?
A most welcome return and a good evening, Laertes.
...And to you, Ophelia.
He found us? How?
Hamlet, what's this about?
I could ask you the same, couldn't I?
All this, after you professed to love me.
Of course, I would be a fool to make you choose between me and your family, or to suggest your loyalty was tied to me alone.
Look before you. Your brother was rallying my own people against me.
All this because, of course, he desires to sit the throne himself.
I received some thoughtful advice at your behest, Ophelia, warning me that such a thing might come to pass.
Laertes, I cannot suffer one I do not trust at my court.
I know you'd come after me, sooner or later.
Even with all our efforts to make amends, you made it clear you believed me an unworthy king.
And just like his uncle, he means to have me killed, I'm certain.
Spirit me off into the night as though I was never here.
Denmark will be different this time. I am not a man who desires that blood be spilled.
I need you gone. Not dead. That would have been my uncle's way.
So here is what I offer: banishment. Leave Denmark, never return, and never write to your sister again.
I will leave you in peace as long as we both live. But, should you return...
I'll have you quartered before the entire court.
Never speak to Ophelia again?
Leave everything in Elsinore behind? ...Would that you'd merely killed me.
This is the end of my life.
How can I be certain you'd keep my father safe?
I shan't. Your father will go with you.
The both of you shall remain in exile until your dying breath.
And what of my sister?
I love Ophelia more fiercely than anyone in this world.
I would rather die than allow her to suffer.
I care deeply that no harm comes to Ophelia. More deeply, apparently, than you do.
That's why once you've gone, you must not contact her.
If you maintain a correspondence, she'll only want to join you all the more. And that will never come to pass.
And I need her here, with me, on the throne, with her mind fully focused on ruling our country.
Her advice is invaluable. She's going to be twice the advisor your father ever was.
What? Hamlet, surely that cannot be necessary.
I'm sparing his life. That's generosity enough.
Your father's old estate awaits you on the borderlands to the south. The estate is barren, but the land is fertile and warm in the winters.
You will be well cared for—but you will not be permitted to leave that estate, nor have correspondence with anyone outside its walls.
And you must be gone before dawn.
Make haste, Laertes.
I failed you. I'm sorry.
Hamlet, there must be another way. Isn't there any way you can be convinced?
...Not this time.
Men, escort him to his chambers, and there ensure he takes all that is his.
And Lord Polonius as well. He must be gone the very same moment his son departs.
This is how things end in this world?
It's the same, every time.
That's the herald's horn. It's... likely Hamlet calling me to make an announcement.
Friends, family, a word, if I may.
Some of you have offered invaluable advice to me over the last few days.
For your assistance, I hold you dearly in my hearts, and highly in my regard.
Some of the best advice I received was of matters concerning the heart.
I... love Ophelia. I've loved her since we were children.
And now she has agreed to take my hand and become my wife. And someday, your Queen.
T-that's... wonderful news, Hamlet.
Aye! Congrats, to the both o' you!
I never thought I'd see the day a woman agreed to marry you of her own free will. But...
If anyone can handle the likes of you, it must be her.
So they managed to reconcile after all.
I suppose that's for the best.
Are you all right, my dear?
Y-yes, fine—
(I can already feel something pulling me. This world won't last.)
(It seems as though when things become quiet... the timeline comes to an end.)
Everyone, we'll prepare a magnificent ceremony for seven days hence. And when we are wed...
Peace will finally come to Denmark. Now, and forevermore.
(Oh, no. Here it comes.)
(But I can return here—if I need to.)
(I could use the Book of Fates to choose this world forever.)
Forced back to the past.

source: My lord, I heard you were seeking advice. Is that so?
I am. What can you tell me of ruling, Bernardo?
You've proven yourself to be a great strategic commander.
I'm sure that sort of skill will become useful in the near future.
Hmm. If there's one thing I've learned through my time in this position...
It's that one must never show weakness or vulnerability.
My father taught me that, and he was the strongest man I knew—outside of your own father, of course.
Presently, the Danish nobility has demonstrated quite a threat to your rule.
With rumors of spies, wartime treason, and other efforts underfoot... it's time they were quieted once more.
Only a show of force will make them acknowledge the true legitimacy of the throne.
But don't the nobility possess a greater standing army than ours? What if they go to war with us?
Then we shall fight them, and show them we aren't afraid.
(That's terrible advice. I expected better of Bernardo.)
(If Brit's family is working with Fortinbras against us, then we've no hope of beating the nobles.)
(I wonder if there's anyone who can encourage Hamlet to form an alliance instead...)
Well, well. Looking for kingly advice, are we?
For the moment, yes.
I've spent my whole life listening to my father's machinations through the walls.
I'm a wealth of advice. Just ask me!
I know the nobility is... unhappy with the Danish throne. What do you believe I should do to make amends?
Well, you've definitely got no hope of overpowering them. And they won't be thrilled that you've decided to take your uncle's place.
As you obviously know, the Danish throne is elected, not ascended. And after two failed candidates from your lineage... well, it might be time for a change!
But. Hmmm.
But what?
An alliance. It's the only way.
Start listening to the nobility, including my father. Ask them what they need, and promise to help them achieve it.
Most of them simply want their coffers full of gold. If you can make that happen, all this nonsense with Fortinbras will blow over.
My father and Claudius always had an uneasy relationship with your father and his ilk.
But I am not like them.
That's a good thing. Just be smart about it.
And be forewarned that if you start to speak with the nobility, you may need to watch for disloyalty within Elsinore.
After all, some of these courtesans have made their careers trying to keep the nobility stamped down for decades. They'll be rightfully upset if you make nice.
You've given me much food for thought. Thanks, Lady Brit.
My prince. I heard you were looking for advice.
O-oh. Irma. I hadn't expected... Well... very well. What would you like to tell me?
You may not recognize my wisdom or respect my age, but Ophelia is a smart lass. She knows better.
Tell me, Prince. Do you know what my life was before I became your mother's faithful servant?
I cannot say I do, nor that it has ever crossed my mind.
They called me Lady Asmodeus, after the demon who mans the baccarat tables at Satan's side.
My gambling-house was the largest in the city, with hundreds of fine men and women passing through my doors each night.
Many of them came to cast dice, play cards, or drink without the watchful eye of their loved ones over them!
I was feared and loathed by every guard in town. And yet, they did nothing to stop me. Do you know why?
I'll bite. Why didn't they stop you?
Because they needed me more than I needed to operate in their city. And because I was a professional.
One can get away with horrible deeds and distasteful behavior if one offers a... necessary service in a clear-cut way.
Someone must always pour the cheap drink and deal the cards, no matter how loud the priests cry about its sinful nature.
If they were to chase me out of town, then what? Some other man or woman would surely come along and do the same!
Better they come to sit at my table, knowing full well where to find me and what my services were.
So must you be with the nobility of Denmark. They both hate and fear the reach offered by the throne.
If you can show them you are sweet if beloved, but vile if spurned, they will avail themselves of you... and see no need to replace you.
